source.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; Harshvardhan Saini; Zhao-Qian Yao; Zheng Lin; Yi-Zhen Liao; Jing-Yi Cui; Yi-Sen Wang; Mengnan Du; Dian-Bo Liu

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly analyzes polysemantic patterns in sparse dictionary learning (SDL) features and argues that SDL optimization can produce them even when the latent dimension is at least the number of ground-truth features. Its results concern learned SDL features, not the original individual neurons discussed in the claim, so they refine the claim’s scope and proposed mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper’s central results concern learned SAE/SDL features, rather than measuring the polysemanticity of individual neurons in the underlying trained models. Table 1 and Table 2 report feature-recovery metrics, not a direct count or rate of polysemantic units; those rows are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. The paper also cites earlier work on polysemanticity, absorption, and neuron resampling; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's results are about latents of sparse dictionary models (SAEs, transcoders, crosscoders) trained on representations. It does not measure the neurons of the base networks that the versions name. Theorem 3.6 shows that polysemantic partial minima can exist in SDL optimization even when nq ≥ n. It is an existence result for auxiliary dictionary latents, with no rate of occurrence and no claim about base-model neurons. The CLIP examples are likewise SAE features. Superposition and polysemanticity serve as the motivating premise. The empirical results report the performance of the authors' own feature-anchoring method. So this is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state that SDL is piecewise biconvex. Its global solution set is underdetermined, with zero-loss solutions that recover no ground-truth features. They report that dead-neuron resampling helps escape partial minima (lower final loss on a Llama 3.1 8B SAE).
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a theoretical SDL framework and feature-anchoring method, rather than reproducing the cited circuit-neuron visualizations or SoLU experiments. Its empirical evaluations focus on learned sparse-dictionary features.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differing feature-recovery outcomes across SDL methods and feature anchoring conditions. It also studies superposition ratio, interference, sparsity, and TopK activation parameter in Appendix G; these are feature-recovery results, not direct measurements of polysemantic-unit share.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3.6: every realizable polysemantic activation pattern that partitions the features gives a positive-loss partial minimum of the SDL loss, even with nq ≥ n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary learning can converge to spurious polysemantic latents even when its dictionary has enough units for every ground-truth feature.

fits_no_version.finding: Without anchoring, Matryoshka SAE features on CLIP mix concepts (e.g. various screens, various boxes). With anchoring, the features shown look monosemantic (qualitative, Appendix H).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining some SDL latents to known concept directions yields more monosemantic dictionary features.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature anchoring raises ground-truth feature recovery and MIP across SDL methods on synthetic and CLIP data. Gains are small for TopK-family methods on synthetic data and larger on CLIP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature anchoring improves SDL feature recovery, with size depending on method and dataset.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says scripts will be provided upon acceptance
record.problems: The empirical recovery metrics do not directly measure polysemanticity. The CLIP experiment lacks explicit ground-truth features and uses class-mean embeddings as proxies. The theoretical results rely on representation assumptions and, for several results, extreme sparsity; the authors note that convergence to global minima is not established. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and the paper does not measure task-performance costs of feature anchoring.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for Appendix G Tables 4–7: these are additional feature-recovery metrics under varying superposition ratio, interference, sparsity, and TopK parameter, not direct measurements of polysemantic-unit share. No rows for the cited prior studies or the Llama SAE resampling loss comparison, which measures training loss/convergence rather than polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No image-classifier neurons (e.g. InceptionV1) are examined. CLIP results concern SAE features, not model neurons.
No share or layer distribution of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models is measured.
Does not test whether base-network neurons are polysemantic because of superposition. Superposition is assumed as a premise.

No measurement of polysemantic neurons arising in base networks from initialization, regularization or noise when capacity suffices. The SDL partial-minimum theorem is an existence result for dictionary latents only.
No base-model activation functions or architectures are varied, and no polysemantic-neuron share or task-performance cost is measured.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Activation range and explanation-scoring choices are not varied.

record.verdict_notes: Original sources (Zoom In, SoLU) are only cited. The 'polysemanticity' studied is that of SAE/transcoder/crosscoder latents, the tool meant to resolve neuron polysemanticity, not the neurons the claim versions describe. The reader's V3 'challenges', V4 'supports' and V5 'supports' labels are removed. A researcher could argue Theorem 3.6 is relevant to V4 by analogy, since an SAE is a two-layer network with enough units. But it proves only that such minima exist, not that training reaches them or how often.

versions.untested_parts: No individual neurons in image classifiers, including InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, are tested.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models, or layer-by-layer comparison of that share, is measured.

The paper analyzes polysemantic activation patterns in SDL features under its theoretical assumptions. It does not establish that individual neurons in trained base networks are packed representations of more features than neurons, or test that as the cause of their polysemanticity.

The paper establishes a theoretical possibility of polysemantic SDL features when latent dimension is at least the number of ground-truth features. It does not isolate initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes, or establish the phenomenon for individual base-network neurons.

The study compares SDL methods and feature anchoring, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons in base models, test SoLU or modern convnets, or measure the cost to the underlying model’s task performance.
It does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons with better tools or test whether their mixed inputs share a feature used by the network.
It does not vary activation-range portions examined or explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

rows.subject: Theoretical SDL framework
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 3.6 constructs a partial minimum for any realizable polysemantic activation pattern that partitions the ground-truth features.

conditions.value: Representation Assumptions; realizable polysemantic pattern forming a partition of [n]

rows.measure: Existence of a partial minimum exhibiting polysemanticity with positive loss
rows.value: Theorem states that such a partial minimum exists
rows.note: The result concerns learned SDL feature activation patterns, not base-model neurons. It shows that these patterns can occur even with nq ≥ n; it does not show how often training reaches them.
rows.check: Theorem 3.6 concerns SDL latents (auxiliary dictionary units), not neurons of trained base networks. It is an existence proof with no measured frequency, so it does not bear on V3 or V4 as worded.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViTB/32 with Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CLIP ImageNet-1K embeddings with feature anchoring versus without it; paper’s qualitative comparison of learned features.
rows.measure: Authors’ qualitative characterization of learned feature semantic coherence
rows.baseline: Without anchoring: features described as polysemantic, with examples combining multiple concepts (e.g. various screens or boxes).
rows.value: With anchoring: features described as monosemantic, with examples for African Grey parrots, American Black Bears, and digital clocks.
rows.note: Qualitative examples and author characterization; no polysemantic-feature rate or task-performance cost is reported.
rows.check: Subject should be the Matryoshka SAE trained on CLIP-ViTB/32 embeddings, not CLIP-ViTB/32 itself. The comparison is the authors' own method (anchoring) against no anchoring on SAE features. It reports no share of polysemantic base-model neurons, so it does not bear on V5.

reader_labels.reason: Theorem 3.6 allows positive-loss polysemantic partial minima even when the latent dimension is at least the number of ground-truth features, so this result does not require a shortage of latent units; it does not test the proposed mechanism in base-model neurons. Row R1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical SDL setting with nq ≥ n
reader_labels.reason: Theorem 3.6 establishes that polysemantic SDL feature patterns can occur with enough latent units, although it does not identify initialization, regularization, or training noise as the cause. Row R1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Matryoshka SAE on CLIP ImageNet-1K embeddings, with versus without feature anchoring
reader_labels.reason: The authors characterize unanchored features as polysemantic and anchored features as monosemantic in their qualitative examples; they do not report a rate or task-performance cost. Row R2.
